article.title: Critical libheif Flaw Cascades Through Sharp Into Unauthenticated RCE in Next.js and Astro's AVIF Image Optimization
article.summary: A critical libheif image-decoding bug inherited through the sharp npm package gave attackers unauthenticated remote code execution via AVIF optimization in Next.js and Astro, patched September 8.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

A critical remote-code-execution vulnerability in libheif — the open-source library used to decode HEIC, HEIF, and AVIF image files — has cascaded through the `sharp` Node.js image-processing package into two popular JavaScript web frameworks, Next.js and Astro. Both frameworks use sharp by default to optimize images, and both shipped fixes on September 8, 2026, after inheriting a flaw that [libheif's own security advisory](https://github.com/strukturag/libheif/security/advisories/GHSA-g89c-p67h-r497) rates 9.8 out of 10 in severity.

## What We Know

### The root cause is a heap buffer overflow in AVIF decoding

The underlying issue, tracked as CVE-2026-84383, is a "[h]eap buffer overflow in `scale_nearest_neighbor()` via duplicate Alpha planes from nested `iden`/`auxl` items," according to [libheif's security advisory](https://github.com/strukturag/libheif/security/advisories/GHSA-g89c-p67h-r497). A specially crafted HEIC, HEIF, or AVIF file can cause the library's image scaler to "write 16-bit samples into an 8-bit Alpha plane allocation, producing a heap buffer overflow," the advisory states, adding that "[t]he overflow size and written values are attacker-controlled via the ISOBMFF container and HEVC bitstream content" and that "[n]o special API options or unusual calling patterns are required." The advisory's impact section states plainly: "We were able to get RCE using this on multiple applications." libheif patched the flaw in version 1.23.2; versions 1.22.0 through 1.23.1 are affected, according to the advisory.

### The flaw reaches Node.js apps through sharp

libheif is not typically installed directly by web developers — it reaches JavaScript projects through `sharp`, an npm package that wraps several native image libraries for server-side image processing. [sharp's security advisory](https://github.com/lovell/sharp/security/advisories/GHSA-rgj7-g3m4-5g8c) says the libheif bug can lead "to possible remote code execution (RCE) on glibc-based Linux when run under certain conditions," and that "[t]hose processing untrusted input with versions of sharp prior to 0.35.4 are affected." sharp's own advisory carries a lower "High" rating — CVSS4 8.9 rather than Critical — but only because, as the advisory explains, "the attack vector for these claims to be 'network' however sharp does not provide any networking features so this vulnerability is down-rated to a 'High' severity using CVSSv4." sharp 0.35.4 bundles the fixed libheif 1.23.2, per the advisory.

### Astro and Next.js both use sharp for image optimization, and both inherited a Critical rating

Because Astro's default image service is built on sharp, [Astro's advisory](https://github.com/withastro/astro/security/advisories/GHSA-26w7-cxv4-gfx2) confirms that "[a] vulnerability in `libheif`, used by the default Sharp image service in Astro, can lead to remote code execution when a malicious AVIF image is optimized," adding that "[p]rojects are affected when an attacker can cause Astro to process an untrusted AVIF image." Astro rates the issue Critical, CVSS 9.8, and says "[t]he fix was released in Astro 7.2.8, which requires Sharp 0.35.4."

Next.js uses sharp for its built-in Image Optimization API, and its advisory is titled "Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in Image Optimization API when AVIF files are used." [Next.js's advisory](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/security/advisories/GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4) explains that "[a] vulnerability in the underlying `libheif` library used by `sharp` which Next.js uses for image optimization can lead to remote code execution when AVIF files are optimized," and notes that "[u]ntil a fix has propagated, optimization of AVIF files is disabled" as an interim measure. Next.js shipped fixes in two release lines, versions 15.5.24 and 16.3.3, covering vulnerable versions back to 10.0.0, according to the advisory.

### The disclosures landed within minutes of each other

libheif's own advisory was published August 25, 2026, giving downstream projects a window to update before the issue became widely public. The sharp, Astro, and Next.js advisories were then all published within about five minutes of each other on September 8, 2026 — Next.js at 21:21 UTC, sharp at 21:25 UTC, and Astro at 21:26 UTC — consistent with a coordinated release once the fix had propagated down the dependency chain from libheif to sharp to the frameworks built on top of it.

## What We Don't Know

None of the four advisories say whether the vulnerability was exploited in the wild before patches shipped, or how many production deployments were running vulnerable configurations at disclosure time. Astro credits a reporter identified as "cn-panda" for its finding; libheif's advisory separately credits a finder identified as "rootxharsh" alongside two named coordinators, but neither advisory clarifies whether these represent the same research effort or independent discoveries of the same underlying libheif bug.
